FD vs RD Comparison Calculator

Fixed deposits generate more total interest than recurring deposits for identical annual sums because the entire lump sum compounds from day one. In recurring deposits, interest accumulates incrementally on monthly installments, resulting in lower total yield despite identical nominal rates.

Formula and Calculation Method

Fixed Deposit (FD) and Recurring Deposit (RD) compound interest formulas:

Fixed Deposit Maturity: A = P × (1 + r ÷ n)^(n × t)
Recurring Deposit Maturity: Sum of each monthly deposit M compounded for its individual tenure (t − i)
Standard Banking RD Approximation: A = M × n + M × [n(n + 1) ÷ 2] × (r ÷ 12) (for simple monthly interest)

Step-by-step deposit comparison procedure:

  1. Identify whether capital is available immediately as a lump sum or must be saved incrementally from monthly wages.
  2. Apply the contractual annual bank interest rate (r) and compounding frequency (n, typically quarterly in banking institutions).
  3. Compute FD interest where the total principal generates returns for the entire multi-year duration.
  4. Compute RD interest where each monthly installment earns compounding interest only for its remaining tenure until maturity.
  5. Compare net pre-tax interest earnings, liquidity access, and premature withdrawal penalties.

Worked Example and Step-by-Step Calculation

Worked Comparison: $12,000 Invested over 1 Year at 7.0% Interest
Identical Capital Allocation ($12,000 Total):
  • Option A (FD): $12,000 lump sum deposited on Day 1 at 7.0% quarterly compound interest.
  • Option B (RD): $1,000 deposited monthly for 12 months at 7.0% quarterly compound interest.

1. Fixed Deposit Maturity: $12,000 × (1 + 0.07 ÷ 4)^4 = $12,000 × 1.07186 = $12,862.31.

2. Fixed Deposit Interest Earned: $12,862.31 minus $12,000 = $862.31.

3. Recurring Deposit Maturity: 12 monthly deposits totaling $12,000 generate $459.72 in cumulative interest.

4. Yield Difference: The FD yields $402.59 more interest (+87.6% higher gain) because all $12,000 compounds from month one.

Comparison Verdict: FD Interest = $862.31 | RD Interest = $459.72 | Difference = $402.59 higher for FD

Side-by-Side Comparison Matrix: Fixed Deposit vs Recurring Deposit

This master comparison matrix summarizes structural differences between fixed and recurring bank deposit accounts:

Feature / Parameter Fixed Deposit (FD) Recurring Deposit (RD)
Deposit Mechanism Single upfront lump-sum payment at account opening Fixed periodic monthly installments debited regularly
Ideal Candidate Individuals with idle lump-sum capital or bonuses Salaried employees saving systematically from monthly income
Interest Compounding Base Entire principal earns interest from Day 1 First deposit earns 12 months; last deposit earns only 1 month
Comparative Yield Substantially higher total interest earned Lower total interest earned on identical total principal
Tenure Flexibility 7 days up to 10 years 6 months up to 10 years
Premature Withdrawal Permitted with 0.5% to 1.0% interest rate penalty Permitted with penalty; delayed installment fees apply
Loan Against Deposit Up to 90% to 95% of deposit balance available as overdraft Up to 80% to 90% of accumulated balance available
Tax Deduction at Source Applicable under bank statutory thresholds (Form 16A/15G) Subject to identical tax liability and reporting rules

Common Mistakes, Limitations & Practical Guidance

  • Premature closure of either deposit account incurs interest penalties, reducing the credited interest rate below the original booked coupon.
  • Interest earned on bank deposits is fully taxable according to your applicable marginal income tax bracket, reducing real post-tax yield.
  • Fixed deposit rates are locked; if central bank benchmark rates rise during your tenure, existing deposits cannot capture higher rates without penalty liquidation.

The Mechanics of Compounding: Day-One Deployment vs Staggered Inflows

The mathematical disparity between fixed deposit and recurring deposit returns originates entirely from the timing of capital deployment. In a 12-month fixed deposit, 100 percent of the invested capital generates compound returns across all 365 days. In a 12-month recurring deposit with identical total capital, the average dollar remains invested for only approximately 6.5 months.

Consequently, even when commercial banks offer identical published nominal interest rates on both products (such as 7.0 percent per annum), the actual dollar interest produced by an FD will almost double the interest generated by an RD. However, the recurring deposit serves a distinct behavioral function: enforcing automated financial discipline for income earners who lack an immediate lump sum.

Taxation, Inflation Drag, and Deposit Laddering Strategies

Both FD and RD interest income is treated as ordinary income under most tax regimes. If a saver earns 7 percent nominal interest but sits in a 30 percent marginal tax bracket, the effective net post-tax return is only 4.9 percent. When headline inflation runs at 5 percent, the real economic return becomes negative.

To optimize liquidity and hedge against interest rate fluctuations, sophisticated savers employ deposit laddering. Rather than committing $50,000 into a single 5-year fixed deposit, the capital is divided into five $10,000 tranches maturing in 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 years respectively. As each tranche matures annually, it is rolled over into a new 5-year deposit at prevailing rates, providing predictable liquidity and rate averaging.

Three Practical Deposit Strategy Scenarios

Scenario 1: Salaried Professional Saving for Vacation (RD)

A software developer plans a $6,000 European vacation in 12 months. Lacking an immediate lump sum, they establish a monthly recurring deposit of $500 at 6.5 percent interest. By automating the monthly transfer on payday, they accumulate the full $6,000 principal plus $213 in net interest, preventing reliance on high-interest credit cards.

Scenario 2: Annual Bonus Deployment into Fixed Deposit (FD)

An executive receives a year-end bonus of $25,000 earmarked for a home down payment in three years. Placing the entire $25,000 into a 3-year fixed deposit at 7.2 percent quarterly compounding yields $5,961 in guaranteed pre-tax interest, growing the down payment fund to $30,961 with zero equity market risk.

Scenario 3: Emergency Fund Hybrid Structure

A family maintaining a $15,000 emergency reserve allocates $10,000 into a 1-year auto-renewing fixed deposit (yielding higher rates while offering 90 percent overdraft credit line availability) and establishes an ongoing $250 monthly RD to systematically replenish cash reserves against inflation.

Frequently Asked Questions About FD vs RD Comparison Calculator

Which gives more interest: FD or RD?

Fixed deposits yield more total interest than recurring deposits for identical total invested capital and identical interest rates because the entire lump sum compounds from day one, whereas RD deposits earn interest gradually.

Are interest rates the same for FD and RD accounts?

Most retail commercial banks offer identical or very similar nominal interest rates for fixed and recurring deposits of equivalent tenure, although senior citizen incentives apply equally to both.

Can I withdraw money prematurely from an FD or RD?

Yes. Most banks permit premature withdrawal, but charge an interest penalty (typically 0.5% to 1.0% below the contractual rate). For recurring deposits, missing monthly installment deadlines may also incur penalty charges.

How is interest calculated on fixed deposits?

Fixed deposit interest is traditionally calculated and compounded on a quarterly basis, adding accumulated interest to principal every three months before maturity payout.

Is interest earned on FD and RD taxable?

Yes. Interest income from both fixed and recurring deposits is fully taxable according to your applicable marginal income tax bracket, and banks may deduct tax at source (TDS) if interest exceeds statutory limits.

Which option is better for monthly salaried individuals?

Recurring deposits are optimal for salaried earners without immediate lump sums, providing automated monthly savings discipline. If you already have a cash lump sum available, a fixed deposit is mathematically superior.
